implementation_notes: LINQ's Select is the map of .NET: an extension method on IEnumerable<TSource> that projects every element with a selector and returns IEnumerable<TResult>; Microsoft's documentation states the result 'contains the same number of elements as the source' and that sequence-returning operators use deferred execution - the query object 'stores all the information that is required to perform the action' and runs only when it is enumerated. It replaces the foreach-with-a-new-list loop, and SelectMany is the flattening step for selectors that themselves return sequences. Keep the hand-written loop for index-dependent or stateful passes; Nullable<T> and Task<T> have no Select, so their mapping stays explicit (HasValue branch, ContinueWith/await).
pitfalls: Deferred execution re-runs the query on every enumeration, so a selector with side effects fires per traversal and captured variables keep their live values.
Select does not flatten: a selector returning a collection yields IEnumerable<IEnumerable<T>>, which is the signal that SelectMany (bind) is what the code needs.
Nullable<T> and Task<T> have no Select: mapping an optional value type means an explicit HasValue branch, and mapping a task means ContinueWith/await plus completion-exception unwrapping.

variants.name: Select over IQueryable<T> (expression tree translated by the provider)
variants.implementation_notes: The same map exists for the query context: Queryable.Select takes an Expression<Func<TSource, TResult>> instead of a delegate, so the projection is data - an expression tree the provider (EF Core, LINQ to SQL, OData) translates into the target language instead of executing in memory. Microsoft's Queryable documentation describes the method as projecting each element into a new form and returning an IQueryable<TResult> whose execution is deferred. Prefer it whenever the source is a database or another remote store; the price is the translatable subset, so a selector calling an arbitrary .NET method either throws or silently moves the rest of the query to client evaluation.
pitfalls: Only the translatable subset works: a local method, a captured object or a string-format call inside the selector can move evaluation to the client, so the query runs differently from what the code implies.
Client-side evaluation over a large set is a silent performance cliff - IQueryable looks like IEnumerable and the difference surfaces only in the SQL log or on the wire.
Expression trees cannot contain statement bodies or assignment: the selector must be an expression, not an arbitrary lambda body, which constrains how the mapper is written.
